title: Opening blind eyes
hook: blessings for sight, freedom, clothing and steady steps

segments.voice: Yesterday, sechvi, the rooster's understanding, the first blessing of the morning. Your line was tell day from night. Today, the eyes open.

Your eyes open in the morning and the room comes back: ceiling, curtain, the chair with yesterday's clothes on it. It takes half a second, and you've done it every day of your life. The prayer book doesn't call that half second waking up. It calls it opening the eyes of the blind. And it keeps going in that key. Sitting up becomes setting the captive free. Getting dressed becomes clothing the naked. Big words, the words of rescue, for the smallest motions of a morning.
screen: `THE ROOM COMES BACK.` → `OPENING THE EYES OF THE BLIND.` → `BIG WORDS FOR SMALL MOTIONS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in Berakhot, pairs each blessing with a motion. When you open your eyes: blessed are you, pokeach ivrim, who opens the eyes of the blind. When you sit up and stretch: matir asurim, who frees the bound, because a body stiff from sleep has just been let loose. When you dress: malbish arumim, who clothes the naked. When you stand up straight: zokef kefufim, who raises the bowed down. When you start to walk: who makes firm a person's steps. Several of these phrases are lifted almost word for word from the Psalms. Psalm one hundred forty-six, in the old Jewish translation, says: "The LORD looseth the prisoners; the LORD openeth the eyes of the blind; the LORD raiseth up them that are bowed down." In the psalm, those are rescues: God lifting the people who have the least. The prayer book borrows that language for your ordinary morning. Why? The Talmud elsewhere calls sleep a sixtieth part of death. Seen that way, every waking is a small return, from not seeing to seeing, from lying still to moving. Many people hear a second layer too. To say who opens the eyes of the blind is to remember that for some people sight is not a given, and freedom isn't, and clothing isn't. The blessing thanks God for your morning in words that keep other people's mornings in view.
screen: `POKEACH IVRIM: WHO OPENS BLIND EYES.` · `A BLESSING FOR EACH MOTION.` · `BORROWED FROM PSALM 146.` · `YOUR MORNING, AND OTHERS' MORNINGS.` · then, large: `EYES OPENED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a few breaths, then open them slowly, as if for the first time today, and let your gaze land on one thing: a cup, a plant, a patch of light, your own hand. Look longer than you normally would, at its color, its edges, its shadow. If you pray, you can say pokeach ivrim; if not, just keep looking.
Pokeach ivrim. Who opens the eyes of the blind — the morning blessing for sight, borrowed word for word from a psalm about rescue.
Your line: eyes opened. The smallest motions of a morning get the words of rescue. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: These blessings are part of the morning blessings said at home on waking or at the start of the morning service, and in many synagogues the leader chants them aloud while the congregation answers amen.

chat.says: Why does the waking prayer say opens the eyes of the blind? I'm not blind.
options: It borrows a psalm's rescue words for waking, and remembers people who can't see.
It's said only by blind people; everyone else skips that line of the blessings.
It's left over from Temple days, when blind people came to be healed at dawn.
chat.meaning: The phrases come from Psalm 146's rescues; waking is a small return, and the words remember those for whom sight isn't given.
